title: Zero, and the Conditions Attached
paragraphs: In April 1911 the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes, working in Leiden, cooled a thread of mercury to a few degrees above absolute zero and watched its electrical resistance vanish.
He could do this because in 1908 he had become the first person to liquefy helium, which boils at about 4.2 kelvin.

Physicists had long argued about what a metal's resistance would do near absolute zero: Lord Kelvin expected it to climb toward infinity as the electrons froze in place, others expected a smooth slide to zero, and still others expected a floor set by impurities.
Mercury did none of these things: its resistance fell gradually and then, within a narrow band near 4.2 kelvin, dropped abruptly to a value too small to measure.
Onnes named the state superconductivity and received the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics, mainly for the low-temperature work behind it.
The word zero is meant literally.
A current started in a copper ring dies away in a fraction of a second as collisions turn its energy into heat.
A current started in a superconducting ring has been followed for years with no measurable decay.

The temperature below which this happens is called the critical temperature, and for the metals Onnes knew it is painfully low: about 4.2 kelvin for mercury, 7.2 for lead, and 9.2 for niobium, the highest of any pure element at ordinary pressure.
The best ordinary conductors never join the club: copper, silver, and gold have not been seen to superconduct at any temperature yet reached.
Superconductivity is thus not good conduction carried to an extreme but a different condition of matter.
Onnes saw the practical prize at once.
A coil with no resistance could carry a huge current without heating and produce a field far stronger than any iron magnet, and he spoke openly of building such magnets.
The hope collapsed almost immediately.

A magnetic field above a modest threshold, now called the critical field, destroyed the superconducting state, and so did a current above a critical value, since a current produces a field of its own.
For lead and mercury the critical field is a small fraction of a tesla, far below what a useful magnet would need.
The second surprise came in 1933, when Walther Meissner and Robert Ochsenfeld in Berlin measured the magnetic field around tin and lead samples cooled through their transitions.
The field was pushed out of the interior: a superconductor is not merely a perfect conductor but a perfect diamagnet, one that expels magnetic flux.
The distinction is subtle, and to my mind it is the deeper of the two discoveries.
A perfect conductor cooled in a magnetic field would simply trap whatever flux was already inside it, because currents induced at its surface would oppose any change.
A superconductor does something a perfect conductor cannot: it expels the field even when it was cooled with the field already present.
The expulsion is not always total.
In pure metals such as lead the field is kept out completely until the critical field is reached, and then superconductivity collapses all at once; these are type I superconductors.

In many alloys and compounds, by contrast, the field enters above a lower critical field, but only as thin threads, each carrying one quantum of flux, and superconductivity survives between the threads up to an upper critical field of many teslas; these are type II.
Type II behavior is why hospital MRI magnets are wound from a niobium-titanium alloy, which stays superconducting in fields of several teslas at about 4 kelvin, the temperature of liquid helium.
Explaining any of this took forty-six years.
Albert Einstein, Niels Bohr, and Werner Heisenberg each tried and failed, and by the 1950s the problem had a reputation for embarrassing theorists.
The decisive clue came in 1950 from experiments on isotopes of mercury: samples with heavier nuclei had a slightly lower critical temperature.
Electrons should not care about nuclear mass unless the nuclei are moving, so the result pointed to vibrations of the crystal lattice.
In 1957 John Bardeen, Leon Cooper, and John Robert Schrieffer assembled the theory that now carries their initials.

In the BCS picture an electron moving through the lattice tugs nearby positive ions toward it, leaving a brief patch of extra positive charge that draws in a second electron, so two electrons that should repel each other end up weakly bound in a Cooper pair.
The pairs settle into one collective quantum state, an energy gap opens above it, and because scattering a single electron would require breaking a pair, the current flows undisturbed.
The three shared the 1972 Nobel Prize in Physics, Bardeen's second; he remains the only person to have won it twice.
The theory proved sound for every superconductor then known, explaining the isotope effect, the energy gap, and the Meissner effect at once.
It also seemed to set a ceiling.

Pairing by lattice vibrations is fragile, and most theorists concluded that it could not survive much above 30 kelvin, so the slow climb of the record, to about 23 kelvin in a niobium-germanium compound by 1973, looked like the approach to a wall.
Liquid helium, scarce and expensive, would always be required.
In 1986 Georg Bednorz and Alex Muller, at an IBM laboratory near Zurich, reported superconductivity at about 35 kelvin in a ceramic oxide of lanthanum, barium, and copper.
Ceramics are usually insulators, and few had thought to look there, so the result met disbelief until other groups reproduced it.
The pair received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1987, the year after the discovery, unusually fast.
Early in 1987 Paul Chu of the University of Houston and Maw-Kuen Wu of the University of Alabama in Huntsville replaced lanthanum with the smaller atom yttrium and found a transition above 90 kelvin.
The number mattered because liquid nitrogen boils at 77 kelvin and is cheap, costing about what milk does.
A hastily arranged session at the American Physical Society's March 1987 meeting drew some two thousand physicists and ran past three in the morning; it is still called the Woodstock of physics.
What followed was a wave of prediction: levitating trains, power grids with no losses, and cheap medical magnets were all said to be a few years away.
Looking back, I think the excitement was earned and the timetables were not.

The copper oxide superconductors, or cuprates, are brittle ceramics that cannot be drawn into wire as niobium-titanium can, and current is weakened where it crosses the boundaries between crystal grains.
Some promises have been kept in modest form: superconducting cables now carry power beneath a few cities, and cuprate filters have been used in cellular base stations.
The record at ordinary pressure, about 133 kelvin in a mercury-based cuprate found in 1993, has not moved since.
There is a deeper embarrassment.
The cuprate electrons do form pairs, but nearly four decades on there is still no agreed account of what holds them together, and few believe lattice vibrations alone can do it at such temperatures.
Meanwhile the old BCS mechanism has staged a comeback.

In 2015 a group in Mainz, Germany, squeezed hydrogen sulfide to about 150 gigapascals, roughly a million and a half atmospheres, and found a critical temperature near 203 kelvin; a lanthanum hydride reached about 250 kelvin a few years later.
These hydrides appear to be conventional BCS superconductors in which light hydrogen atoms vibrate fast enough to bind pairs tightly, the loophole the 30 kelvin argument overlooked.

They are also useless outside a diamond anvil, and I would urge caution about the headlines that greet each new record: several recent claims of room-temperature superconductivity have been withdrawn after other laboratories could not reproduce them and questions arose about the data.
More than a century after Leiden, the pattern is hard to miss.
The experiments came first, usually in a cold corner of a laboratory, and theory followed, sometimes by decades.
Each advance arrived from an unlikely direction: a poor conductor like mercury, an insulating ceramic, a gas crushed between diamonds.
That is worth remembering the next time someone announces that the search for a room-temperature superconductor has reached its limit.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Lord Kelvin expected that near absolute zero a metal's electrical resistance would
choices: fall smoothly to zero as the metal cooled
rise toward infinity as the electrons froze in place
level off at a floor set by impurities
vanish abruptly within a narrow band of temperature near 4.2 kelvin
depend on the mass of the atoms' nuclei

proof.quote: Lord Kelvin expected it to climb toward infinity as the electrons froze in place

questions.why: Paragraph 1 lays out three old predictions and attaches Kelvin's name to one of them: resistance climbing toward infinity as the electrons froze in place.
distractorNotes: Wrong camp: paragraph 1 gives the smooth slide to zero to unnamed others, not to Kelvin.
Wrong camp: the floor set by impurities is the third prediction in paragraph 1, not Kelvin's.
This is what mercury actually did, which paragraph 1 says matched none of the predictions.
Wrong paragraph: the dependence on nuclear mass is the 1950 isotope result in paragraph 6.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which pure element has the highest critical temperature at ordinary pressure?
choices: mercury
lead
copper
niobium
tin

proof.quote: 9.2 for niobium, the highest of any pure element at ordinary pressure

questions.why: Paragraph 2 lists the metals Onnes knew and names niobium, at 9.2 kelvin, as the highest of any pure element at ordinary pressure.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 2 puts mercury at about 4.2 kelvin, the lowest of the three listed.
Paragraph 2 puts lead at 7.2 kelvin, below niobium.
Paragraph 2 says copper has not been seen to superconduct at all.
Tin appears in paragraph 4 as a Meissner sample; no critical temperature is given for it.

questions.stem: The author mentions copper, silver, and gold in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: show that superconductivity is not simply ordinary conduction carried further
explain why Onnes chose mercury rather than a more familiar metal
list the metals whose critical temperatures had been measured by 1911
argue that the best conductors will eventually be found to superconduct
illustrate how impurities set a floor beneath the resistance of ordinary metals

proof.quote: copper, silver, and gold have not been seen to superconduct
not good conduction carried to an extreme but a different condition of matter

questions.why: Right after naming the three best ordinary conductors, paragraph 2 draws the lesson: superconductivity is not good conduction carried to an extreme but a different condition of matter. The three metals are there to make that point.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: paragraph 1 never says why Onnes chose mercury.
Reversed: these are metals that have not been seen to superconduct, so they have no critical temperature to list.
Too strong and reversed: the passage says they have never been seen to superconduct and makes no prediction that they will.
Wrong paragraph: the impurity floor is one of the pre-1911 predictions in paragraph 1.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a wire of pure niobium would
choices: superconduct in liquid nitrogen but not in liquid helium
lose its resistance at a higher temperature than any cuprate
carry a persistent current only if its crystal contains defects
stay superconducting in a field of several teslas
superconduct in liquid helium but not in liquid nitrogen

proof.quote: 9.2 for niobium
helium, which boils at about 4.2 kelvin
liquid nitrogen boils at 77 kelvin

questions.why: Paragraph 2 puts niobium's critical temperature at 9.2 kelvin. Paragraph 1 says liquid helium boils at about 4.2 kelvin, cold enough, and paragraph 8 says liquid nitrogen boils at 77 kelvin, far too warm.
distractorNotes: Reversed: 77 kelvin is well above niobium's 9.2 kelvin, while 4.2 kelvin is below it.
Reversed: paragraphs 8 and 9 put cuprate transitions above 90 kelvin and up to about 133 kelvin, far above 9.2.
Outside the passage: nothing links persistent currents to crystal defects.
Unsupported: paragraph 3 says pure metals lose superconductivity in modest fields; several teslas is credited only to the niobium-titanium alloy in paragraph 5.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Onnes's hope of building powerful magnets collapsed because
choices: liquid helium could not be produced in quantities large enough to cool a coil
the mercury he used could not be drawn into a wire
modest magnetic fields destroyed the superconducting state
the current in his coils died away within a fraction of a second
iron magnets turned out to be stronger than any coil he could build

proof.quote: A magnetic field above a modest threshold, now called the critical field, destroyed the superconducting state

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the hope collapsed almost immediately because a field above a modest threshold destroyed the superconducting state, and a coil's own current makes a field.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: nothing is said about a shortage of liquid helium in Leiden.
Wrong paragraph: trouble drawing wire belongs to the cuprates in paragraph 9, not to Onnes's magnets.
Wrong paragraph: a current dying away in a fraction of a second is the copper ring of paragraph 2.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the coil would be far stronger than any iron magnet; the problem was the field, not the iron.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a superconductor differs from a perfect conductor in that a superconductor
choices: expels a field even when cooled with that field already inside
traps whatever magnetic flux was present when it was cooled
allows a magnetic field to die away gradually within its interior
carries a persistent current for years with no measurable decay
keeps a magnetic field out only until a critical field is reached

proof.quote: it expels the field even when it was cooled with the field already present
A perfect conductor cooled in a magnetic field would simply trap whatever flux was already inside it

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says a perfect conductor cooled in a field would simply trap the flux inside it, while a superconductor expels the field even when it was cooled with the field already present. That is the difference Meissner and Ochsenfeld found.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 4 says trapping the flux is what a perfect conductor would do.
Outside the passage: nothing says the field fades gradually inside the material.
Not a difference: zero resistance is shared by both, and paragraph 4 says a superconductor is not merely a perfect conductor.
Half right: paragraph 5 says type I materials keep the field out until the critical field, but that is not what separates them from a perfect conductor.

questions.stem: A laboratory cools a new material below the temperature at which its resistance vanishes while a weak magnetic field, well below any critical field, passes through it, and finds the field inside the sample unchanged after cooling. Based on the reasoning in paragraph 4, the laboratory should conclude that the material
choices: is a type II superconductor in which flux has entered as thin threads
has a critical temperature above the boiling point of liquid helium
has reached its upper critical field and lost superconductivity
is behaving as a perfect conductor rather than as a superconductor
is a type I superconductor cooled below its critical temperature

proof.quote: A perfect conductor cooled in a magnetic field would simply trap whatever flux was already inside it
it expels the field even when it was cooled with the field already present

questions.why: Paragraph 4 gives the test: a perfect conductor cooled in a field traps the flux, while a superconductor expels it even when cooled with the field present. A field that stays unchanged is the perfect-conductor result, so the sample has not shown the Meissner effect.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: paragraph 5 says the field enters a type II material only above a lower critical field, and the stem says the field is well below any critical field, so a superconductor should have expelled it.
Unrelated: nothing in the case says what coolant was used or where the transition sits.
Contradicted: the stem says the field is well below any critical field, and losing superconductivity would mean the resistance returned.
Contradicted: paragraph 5 says a type I superconductor keeps the field out completely below its critical field, not unchanged inside.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that MRI magnets are wound from a niobium-titanium alloy rather than from pure lead or mercury because
choices: the alloy has a critical temperature well above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen
the alloy remains superconducting in fields that would destroy the pure metals
lead and mercury cannot be cooled below their critical temperatures with helium
the alloy is a type I superconductor that expels fields completely
pure metals have too few crystal defects to carry a persistent current

proof.quote: For lead and mercury the critical field is a small fraction of a tesla, far below what a useful magnet would need
stays superconducting in fields of several teslas

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says lead and mercury lose superconductivity in a small fraction of a tesla, far below what a useful magnet needs, and paragraph 5 says the niobium-titanium alloy stays superconducting in fields of several teslas. The field tolerance is the difference.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 5 says the alloy works at about 4 kelvin, the temperature of liquid helium, far below nitrogen's 77 kelvin.
Contradicted: paragraph 2 puts lead and mercury at 7.2 and 4.2 kelvin, and Onnes reached those temperatures with liquid helium.
Reversed: paragraph 5 says the alloys and compounds that tolerate high fields are type II, not type I.
Outside the passage: nothing links persistent currents to crystal defects.

questions.stem: The author mentions Einstein, Bohr, and Heisenberg in paragraph 6 primarily to
choices: credit the physicists whose early ideas led to the BCS theory
show that the isotope experiments of 1950 confirmed their predictions
suggest that theorists had lost all interest in superconductivity by the 1950s
contrast the fame of these physicists with the obscurity of Bardeen
convey how difficult the problem of explaining superconductivity had proved

proof.quote: each tried and failed, and by the 1950s the problem had a reputation for embarrassing theorists
Explaining any of this took forty-six years.

questions.why: Paragraph 6 opens by saying the explanation took forty-six years, then names three of the most famous physicists of the century and says each tried and failed. The names measure the difficulty.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the passage says they failed; it does not connect their ideas to BCS.
Wrong link: paragraph 6 says the isotope effect pointed to lattice vibrations, not to anything these three predicted.
Too strong: a problem that embarrasses theorists is one they keep attacking, and BCS arrived in 1957.
Outside the passage: Bardeen is presented as a two-time Nobel winner, hardly obscure.

questions.stem: All of the following are described in the passage as part of the BCS picture EXCEPT:
choices: a passing electron tugs nearby positive ions toward itself
two electrons become weakly bound into a Cooper pair
the two electrons attract each other through their charges
an energy gap separates the paired state from any excited state
scattering a single electron would require breaking a pair

proof.quote: tugs nearby positive ions toward it
weakly bound in a Cooper pair
an energy gap opens above it
scattering a single electron would require breaking a pair
two electrons that should repel each other

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the two electrons should repel each other; what binds them is the patch of positive charge left in the lattice, not any attraction between their own charges. The other four statements are all in paragraph 6.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 6 says the electron tugs nearby positive ions toward it.
Paragraph 6 ends its description with the electrons weakly bound in a Cooper pair.
Paragraph 6 says an energy gap opens above the collective state.
Paragraph 6 says scattering a single electron would require breaking a pair.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, the word 'sound' most nearly means
choices: audible
well founded
straightforward
popular
undamaged

proof.quote: The theory proved sound for every superconductor then known

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says the theory proved sound and then lists what it explained at once; the sentence is about the theory holding up, so sound means well founded.
distractorNotes: Audible is the noise meaning of the word, and nothing in the sentence is heard.
Simplicity is not what the sentence tests; it tests whether the theory held up against every known case.
Popularity is not mentioned; the sentence is about the theory explaining the evidence.
Undamaged is a physical sense of the word, as in sound timber, and does not fit a theory.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the 1987 transition above 90 kelvin was reached by
choices: squeezing the lanthanum compound under enormous pressure
reproducing the Zurich result in several laboratories
cooling the lanthanum compound in liquid nitrogen rather than helium
substituting copper for barium in the Zurich ceramic
replacing lanthanum with the smaller atom yttrium

proof.quote: replaced lanthanum with the smaller atom yttrium and found a transition above 90 kelvin

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says Chu and Wu replaced lanthanum with the smaller atom yttrium and found a transition above 90 kelvin.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: squeezing under enormous pressure is the hydride work of paragraph 10.
Reversed sequence: reproduction confirmed the 35 kelvin result; it did not raise the transition.
Reversed cause and effect: the transition above 90 kelvin is what made liquid nitrogen usable, not the other way around.
Mash-up: copper was already part of the Zurich oxide; the substitution in paragraph 8 was yttrium for lanthanum.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the discovery reported by Bednorz and Muller EXCEPT:
choices: It occurred above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
It was made at an IBM laboratory near Zurich.
It involved a ceramic oxide containing copper.
It was met with disbelief when first reported.
It brought the two physicists a Nobel Prize the following year.

proof.quote: at an IBM laboratory near Zurich
a ceramic oxide of lanthanum, barium, and copper
the result met disbelief
received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1987, the year after the discovery
about 35 kelvin
liquid nitrogen boils at 77 kelvin

questions.why: Paragraph 8 puts the Zurich transition at about 35 kelvin and says liquid nitrogen boils at 77 kelvin; it was the yttrium material of 1987 that crossed that line. The other four statements are all in paragraph 8.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 8 opens with the IBM laboratory near Zurich.
Paragraph 8 names a ceramic oxide of lanthanum, barium, and copper.
Paragraph 8 says the result met disbelief until other groups reproduced it.
Paragraph 8 says the pair received the prize in 1987, the year after the discovery.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the predictions that followed the 1987 discoveries is best described as
choices: scornful
nostalgic
measured
indifferent
credulous

proof.quote: I think the excitement was earned and the timetables were not
Some promises have been kept in modest form

questions.why: Paragraph 9 gives the predictions their due, calling the excitement earned, then faults the timetables and tallies what was and was not delivered. That is a measured verdict, neither mocking nor starry-eyed.
distractorNotes: Too harsh: the author says the excitement was earned and credits promises kept in modest form.
Wrong register: the author is weighing the predictions against results, not longing for the moment.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position on both the excitement and the timetables.
Reversed: the author says the timetables were not earned and urges caution about new headlines in paragraph 10.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the hydrogen sulfide experiment of 2015
choices: produced the first superconductor with a critical temperature above 77 kelvin
was carried out at an IBM laboratory in Switzerland
confirmed that lattice vibrations cannot bind pairs above 30 kelvin
required a pressure of roughly a million and a half atmospheres
was later withdrawn when other laboratories could not reproduce it

proof.quote: about 150 gigapascals, roughly a million and a half atmospheres

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the Mainz group squeezed hydrogen sulfide to about 150 gigapascals, roughly a million and a half atmospheres, before finding a transition near 203 kelvin.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: the first material above 77 kelvin was the yttrium cuprate of 1987 in paragraph 8.
Wrong place: paragraph 10 puts the work in Mainz, Germany; the IBM laboratory near Zurich belongs to 1986.
Reversed: paragraph 10 says the hydrides are the loophole the 30 kelvin argument overlooked.
Wrong result: the withdrawn claims in paragraph 10 are room-temperature claims, not the 203 kelvin measurement.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the hydride superconductors matter to theorists mainly because they
choices: show that the cuprates must also be held together by lattice vibrations
show that lattice-mediated pairing can work far above 30 kelvin
prove that a room-temperature superconductor is within reach
confirm that heavier nuclei raise the critical temperature
demonstrate that the Meissner effect disappears under extreme pressure

proof.quote: conventional BCS superconductors in which light hydrogen atoms vibrate fast enough to bind pairs tightly, the loophole the 30 kelvin argument overlooked
most theorists concluded that it could not survive much above 30 kelvin

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says theorists thought pairing by lattice vibrations could not survive much above 30 kelvin. Paragraph 10 then calls the hydrides conventional BCS superconductors near 203 and 250 kelvin and names them the loophole that argument overlooked.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 10 says few believe lattice vibrations alone can explain the cuprates.
Too strong: paragraph 10 says the hydrides are useless outside a diamond anvil and urges caution about room-temperature claims.
Reversed: paragraph 6 says heavier nuclei lowered the critical temperature, and the hydrides work because hydrogen is light.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the Meissner effect under pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: The BCS theory of 1957 explained every superconductor then known, and the discoveries that followed have confirmed rather than challenged its central mechanism
Superconductivity became a practical technology only after the 1987 cuprates made cooling with inexpensive liquid nitrogen possible for the first time
Superconductors have remained laboratory curiosities because they must be kept extremely cold, shielded from strong fields, and limited to small currents
Superconductivity has advanced by experimental surprises that theory struggled to follow, and its promise has arrived more slowly than predicted
Room-temperature superconductivity is now within reach because hydrides under pressure have shown that lattice vibrations can bind pairs at high temperatures

proof.quote: The experiments came first, usually in a cold corner of a laboratory, and theory followed, sometimes by decades.
Each advance arrived from an unlikely direction
the excitement was earned and the timetables were not
Explaining any of this took forty-six years.

questions.why: The passage runs from Leiden to the hydrides and closes by naming the pattern: experiments first, theory following by decades, each advance from an unlikely direction. Along the way it keeps weighing promise against delivery, from Onnes's magnets to the 1987 timetables.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: paragraph 10 says there is still no agreed account of the cuprates, so later discoveries did challenge the mechanism.
Too narrow and contradicted: the MRI magnets in paragraph 5 use a helium-cooled alloy, and paragraph 9 says the cuprates are still hard to use.
Too extreme: paragraphs 5 and 9 describe MRI magnets, power cables, and filters in real use.
Too strong: paragraph 10 says the hydrides are useless outside a diamond anvil and that room-temperature claims have been withdrawn.
